implementation_notes: The C toolchain is the original home of this discipline, and C makes the cost model concrete. Profile with perf (perf record, perf report, perf annotate) or valgrind/callgrind; measure with clock_gettime or rdtsc around a warmed-up loop. In C the micro-optimisations that actually pay are layout (an array of structs vs a struct of arrays, 64-byte alignment so a cache line is not split), avoiding malloc in a hot path, hoisting a pointer chase, and removing a branch the profile shows is mispredicted. The C-specific trap is that -O2 already does much of it, so a hand-unrolled loop often loses to the compiler's own vectoriser - measure, do not assume. gcc -fopt-info-vec reports which loops vectorised, and -march=native changes the baseline the benchmark measures.
idiom_name: perf / valgrind attribution plus clock_gettime or rdtsc benchmarks, applied one change at a time under -O2
pitfalls: Hand-unrolling a loop that -O2 -march=native already vectorises - the compiler's version is usually faster than the hand-unrolled one.
struct padding causing false sharing in a multi-threaded hot field: align it to the cache line, which is a layout change with a measurable payoff.
Benchmarking before the pages are faulted in (the first-touch cost dominates a short run) - warm up the working set first.
A volatile accumulator that defeats the compiler's optimisation as a side effect: use a black-hole sink carefully so the work is neither elided nor serialised.
-march=native changes the baseline: a benchmark run on it may not reflect the production CPU, and it changes what the compiler decides.
